entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17982"/><div sID="gen36801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17982"/><hi type="bold">2. as a thief in the night--</hi>The apostles in this image follow the parable of their Lord, expressing how the Lord's coming shall take men by surprise (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.43">Mt 24:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>). "The night is wherever there is quiet unconcern" [Bengel]. "At midnight" (perhaps figurative: to some parts of the earth it will be literal night), <reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Mt 25:6</reference>. The thief not only gives no notice of his approach but takes all precaution to prevent the household knowing of it. So the Lord (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.15">Re 16:15</reference>). Signs will precede the coming, to confirm the patient hope of the watchful believer; but the coming itself shall be sudden at last (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.32-Matt.24.36">Mt 24:32-36</reference>; Lu 21:25-32, 35). <div eID="gen36801" type="x-p"/>

To sleep by day would imply great indolence; to be drunken by day, great shamelessness. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17988"/><div sID="gen36819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17988"/>8. Faith, hope, and love, are the three pre-eminent graces (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>). We must not only be awake and sober, but also armed; not only watchful, but also guarded. The armor here is only defensive; in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13-Eph.6.17">Ep 6:13-17</reference>, also offensive. Here, therefore, the reference is to the Christian means of being guarded against being surprised by the day of the Lord as a thief in the night. The helmet and breastplate defend the two vital parts, the head and the heart respectively. "With head and heart right, the whole man is right" [Edmunds]. The head needs to be kept from error, the heart from sin. For "the breastplate of righteousness," <reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">Ep 6:14</reference>, we have here "the breastplate of faith and love"; for the righteousness which is imputed to man for justification, is "faith working by love" (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.22-Rom.4.24">22-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>). "Faith," as the motive within, and "love," exhibited in outward acts, constitute the perfection of righteousness. In <reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">Ep 6:17</reference> the helmet is "salvation"; here, "the hope of salvation." In one aspect "salvation" is a present possession (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.24">5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.13">1Jo 5:13</reference>); in another, it is a matter of "hope" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.24">Ro 8:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">25</reference>). Our Head primarily wore the "breastplate of righteousness" and "helmet of salvation," that we might, by union with Him, receive both. <div eID="gen36819" type="x-p"/>

Quench not--</hi>the Spirit being a holy fire: "where the Spirit is, He burns" [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.3">Ac 2:3</reference>; 7:51). Do not throw cold water on those who, under extraordinary inspiration of the Spirit, stand up to speak with tongues, or reveal mysteries, or pray in the congregation. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18001"/><div sID="gen36849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18001"/>21-22. Some of the oldest manuscripts insert "But." You ought indeed not to "quench" the manifestations of "the Spirit," nor "despise prophesyings"; "but," at the same time, do not take "all" as genuine which professes to be so; "prove (test) all" such manifestations. The means of testing them existed in the Church, in those who had the "discerning of spirits" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.29">14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1Jo 4:1</reference>). Another sure test, which we also have, is, to try the professed revelation whether it accords with Scripture, as the noble Bereans did (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.20">Is 8:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>). This precept negatives the Romish priest's assumption of infallibly laying down the law, without the laity having the right, in the exercise of private judgment, to test it by Scripture. Locke says, Those who are for laying aside reason in matters of revelation, resemble one who would put out his eyes in order to use a telescope.<div eID="gen36849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hold fast that which is good--</hi>Join this clause with the next clause (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.22">1Th 5:22</reference>), not merely with the sentence preceding. As the result of your "proving all things," and especially all prophesyings, "hold fast (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.15">Lu 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1Co 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.1">He 2:1</reference>) the good, and hold yourselves aloof from every appearance of evil" ("every evil species" [Bengel and Wahl]). Do not accept even a professedly spirit-inspired communication, if it be at variance with the truth taught you (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36850" type="x-p"/>
